name: Custom PEEK jaw implant
lead: A custom PEEK jaw implant is a patient-specific implant made of polyether ether ketone (PEEK), a semicrystalline thermoplastic, designed from a CT scan to add contour to the jaw. People seek it to build out a recessed chin or a flat or over-resected mandibular angle, giving a stronger, more defined or more symmetrical lower face. PEEK is also used in spinal fusion devices and as a partial skull replacement in neurosurgery.[1]

In published reports, custom PEEK implants have been used as onlays on the chin and mandibular angles, to revise over-resected angles after jaw-angle reduction surgery, and to correct asymmetry after orthognathic surgery.[6][7] In one retrospective series of 24 patients, FACE-Q lower-face scores rose from 42.50 to 56.08 after patient-specific PEEK revision of over-resected mandibles.[6]

PEEK was invented in 1978 and marketed in the early 1980s by a division of ICI that later became Victrex.[1] It is radiolucent, meaning largely transparent to X-rays, and because it is hydrophobic it may not fully fuse with bone.[1] Published research on cosmetic use is mostly small retrospective series and case reports; registered trials of PEEK in the mouth and face cover dental frameworks and facial plates, which are different applications.

paras: Patient-specific implants are planned on a CT-derived 3D model of the patient's jaw and then manufactured to match, in contrast to stock implants that surgeons trim in the operating room. Published workflows describe computer-aided planning, rapid prototyping of PEEK onlay implants and navigation-assisted placement; one early single-patient report measured a mean total error of 0.81 millimetres between planned and achieved position.[6][7]

In a retrospective comparison of 21 patients with mandibular angle contouring, 12 received stock porous polyethylene implants and 9 received PEEK patient-specific implants; surgery was about 15 minutes shorter with the PEEK implants, stock implants needed intraoperative modification, and 3D implants showed somewhat better symmetry that did not reach statistical significance.[6]

PEEK has strong mechanical and chemical resistance, a Young's modulus of about 3.6 GPa and tensile strength of 90-100 MPa, low water absorption (about 0.1 percent over 24 hours), and resistance to degradation.[1] It is machinable and can be injection-moulded or 3D printed, though its complex production makes it expensive.[1]

Other facial implant materials include silicone, which does not bond to surrounding tissue, porous polyethylene (Medpor), where tissue grows into the pores and makes removal harder, and ePTFE, which is screwed to bone with titanium screws.[9] Wikipedia's chin augmentation article does not mention PEEK.[9]

Reported indications include chin recontouring, mandibular angle augmentation, correction of angle defects such as in otomandibular syndrome, revision after over-resection of the angle, and asymmetry after orthognathic surgery.[6][7] A 2025 review of facial implants in orthognathic surgery included 17 studies published between 1998 and 2025.[7]

PEEK was invented in November 1978 and brought to market in the early 1980s by a division of Imperial Chemical Industries; a management buyout of that division created Victrex.[1] Its medical use grew through spinal fusion cages and cranial implants, and patient-specific PEEK facial implants entered the craniofacial literature with computer-aided planning workflows such as a 2014 report in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery.[6]

Published studies are small and mostly retrospective. A retrospective study of 24 patients (39 mandibles) treated between 2019 and 2023 used endoscopic-assisted revision with patient-specific PEEK implants in over-resected mandibles: 96 percent of implants deviated less than 0.3 millimetres from plan, FACE-Q lower-face scores rose from 42.50 to 56.08, and psychological well-being scores from 61.50 to 70.58.[6] A study of six patients receiving seven PEEK onlays (three chins and four angles) found a soft tissue gain of 6.8 millimetres at the chin and 4.42 millimetres at the angle at six months, equal to about 109 percent and 66 percent of planned implant thickness respectively.[6] A 2022 case report described a 25-year-old patient with a right angle defect from otomandibular syndrome with a satisfactory result at 12 months.[6] The comparison with stock porous polyethylene noted infections in both groups without a significant difference.[6]

Registered trials involve related uses: a post-market follow-up of PEKK midface and mandibular plates (n=91, for conditions such as tumour, fractures and fibrous dysplasia),[2] and trials of PEEK frameworks for implant-supported dental prostheses, two of which were terminated early.[3][4][5]

Complications reported in the comparison study included postoperative infection in both the stock and PEEK groups.[6] More generally, chin and jaw implants carry risks of swelling, haematoma, lip weakness or numbness, infection, bony changes, implant displacement and nerve damage, according to Wikipedia's chin augmentation article, which also notes that surgeon experience can reduce complication risk.[9] Because PEEK is hydrophobic and may not fuse with bone, fixation is a consideration in placement.[1]

Mandibular and chin contouring appear in the hardmaxxing part of looksmaxxing culture alongside genioplasty and jaw-angle surgery. No community discussion specific to PEEK implants was available for this article.

card.summary: A patient-specific jaw implant in PEEK plastic; the material is established in spine and skull surgery, but no cosmetic jaw studies were found.
card.note: No clinical studies of cosmetic custom PEEK jaw implants were found.

quick.overview:
A custom PEEK jaw implant is a made-to-measure implant in a rigid medical plastic, discussed as an alternative to other jaw implant materials. PEEK itself has a long record in spinal and cranial implants.

No clinical studies specific to cosmetic jaw augmentation were found.
quick.mechanism: The implant is shaped to a patient's anatomy and placed against or fixed to the jawbone. PEEK is radiolucent and, being hydrophobic, may not fully fuse with bone.
quick.risks: No procedure-specific risk data were found. General implant surgery risks, such as infection and implant displacement, apply to facial implants as described for chin implants.

angle.text: A custom PEEK implant adds bone-like volume at planned points on the chin or jaw angle. It is used by people who want more projection or definition, and by patients whose angles were over-reduced or are asymmetric.
